questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to a country where I to some extend know the language and a country that is not the most popular Erasmus exchange destination. My choosing of Poland was quite spontaneous as I in the beginning did not see that it was on the list over available countries. But as my family is from Poland, as soon as I noticed Poland as a destination, it was a no brainer that I had to go there.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It has now been now been two weeks since I have come back home and it is still difficult to rate my overall experience. I am so thankful for the experience, the friends that I made and the opportunity to get to know the city, but the amount of university work that I had was exceeding my capabilities and my time, which made it difficult to enjoy the semester fully, as I just spent 2 months solely studying in the library.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy if we are talking about the overall "information" I needed in order to settle in Poland. The only thing I struggled a bit with was how to get a transportation card/metro card.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The International relations office, my mobility coordinator in Poland and the Erasmus student network all did a lot to help me answer any questions or bureaucratic difficulties that I had.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Everything was done excellently. I personally only struggled with the process of course registration, but there was always a lot of assistance to be found on that matter.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I have no recommendations as I found my housing through family/friend connections.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Please do your best at finding housing in the city if the city is big. I lived on the outskirts of the city and it was really hard to sit in public transportation for at least 45 min one way in order to get somewhere. Also, have a look whether there is a supermarket near your potential housing. Mine was 4 bus stops away, which made it very challenging to go grocery shopping.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As I said, I have not lived in student housing, but I did go to a student dorm to see a friend, and sorry to say, but that was a disaster. If you want really cheap housing then the student dorms are great, but the kitchens can basically not be called kitchens and there is no such thing as privacy, as you have guards in the lobby controlling who goes where and who has visitors and at what hour. But that dorm was also one of the oldest so also take that into consideration.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Of course there was a lot of bureaucracy, but it was overall very transparent and easy to see what the necessary steps were.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Everything was done on one website and the registration process was divided into a few categories, so you could see which steps to take. Additionally, on the registration site there was also a pdf that showed step by step what to do.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The international relations office.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: That was the thing I struggled the most with. As a psychology student it was a must that I find the exact same courses in Poland as I would have had in Denmark. This made the course search more challenging. Additionally, us psychology students were not allowed to register ourselves because our mobility coordinator had to do it. So he just sent out a google forms questionnaire with all the subjects in English at the faculty of psychology. However, I wanted to take courses in Polish, so I had to email him afterwards to add me to the polish courses. This was a few days before the semester was to begin, so I was scared that I would not get in. Additionally, the courses in Poland are really small, I had courses ranging from 1-4 ECTS points, and because I had to take 30 ECTS points I ended up taking 10 classes.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not worry about the very late registration for classes. Somehow you will get into all your courses. Additionally, be also prepared that many of your courses that you initially choose might not be available. So you will unfortunately have to go through the course catalog many times and probably end up with completely different courses than you expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was way too much work. I had to quit my job in order to find time to do all the required assignments and homework. There were some courses that were really well structured and of very high quality, which I learned so much from, but some were also an educational and pedagogical disaster.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I only took master level classes.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It is completely different. 
1. There is a hierarchy, where the professor is "higher" than you and you have to speak to the professor in a formal way.
2. There is mandatory attendance. 
3. You CANNOT be late. 
4. There is a lot of talk about grades and "points" and extracurricular tasks that you can do in order to gain more points. 

But on the other hand, if you take seminar classes, then the amount of students in the class is smaller, which makes it fore a better and cozier learning environment.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Cross-Cultural Psychology
Introduction to Psychotherapy
People in organizations
Management Principles and Organizational Development
Group work
Organizations in their environment
Coaching as a method	
Philosophy of science: an overview for cognitive science
Critical reading and academic writing
What is school for? Pedagogical theories behind teacher's work

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Group work - IN POLISH - the professor is amazing, so thorough, and pedagogical, and the course is very applicable to other psychological fields. 
Introduction to psychotherapy - IN ENGLISH - the class is demanding, as it is only 3 ECTS and you need to take 3 tests and make a movie, but it is the class I learned the most from.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Public transportation is VERY cheap and groceries as well - but that I expected. 
Eating out, going out and drinking in bars was way cheaper than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was plenty. I just did not participate in it so I cant fully say.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Do things with the Erasmus student Network - they put so much effort into making nice events for exchange students.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Gdansk, Kraków (+ Auschwitz), Zakopane, Wroclaw.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: As I am fluent in Polish it was not difficult for me to find my way around and communicate with others, so yes.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It is difficult. Try to take some classes with them, but other than that I have no advice. They are really kind and open, but they already have their friend groups so they are not that eager to befriend Erasmus students. But that is something I have heard happens in basically all countries.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The respect for professors and elderly people, and the societal hierarchy. It was weird for me to say "professor" to my professors and "sir, madam" to other people. 
It was weird for me that Polish people were not afraid to blatantly stare at you and never smile.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The availability of everything and the overall cheaper lifestyle. As I am Polish it is difficult for me to point out the things I appreciate the most because I am just used to them.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Please do not take too many courses. Look at their requirements and the amount of work you will have to do. 
2. Participate in the "introduction weeks" hosted my the Erasmus Student Network. This is where most people find their friends. 
3. The most valuable thing during an exchange are the connections that you make. So make sure to dedicate some time to your friends. 
4. Say yes.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The connections that I made.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Not giving up due to the academic pressure and the amount of work I had to do for my courses.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I really think that I was put in a rare situation. When I speak to most of my friends from exchange, even those from the faculty of psychology, I seemed to be the only one with that much work. I was the only one who has 12 exams and who had to lock myself in the library. At psychology, the other students also had some things to do, but it could not be compared to the amount of work I had. I think I was really unlucky and I think that the psychology courses at UW are just more demanding. I hope my comments will not scare you away. If so, consider taking a few courses at other faculties - then you can get the "typical" Erasmus courses that are less demanding. Coming from Denmark, where everything is so expensive that you barely enjoy going out to a restaurant or a bar, being in Poland felt like a blessing.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
